Title: Holly (Holly Gibney, #3)
Author: Stephen  King
My Review:
I've returned to Goodreads after a long hiatus specifically to rate this book, which I thought was vaguely entertaining (I finished it, after all!) but regularly frustrated the hell out of me.

It's hard for me to say what exactly annoyed me so much about this book. Sure, the dialogue was pretty bad* at points, but I've enjoyed plenty of novels with bad dialogue. Did I think the constant Covid references and characters asking each other if they were vaccinated was a little tiresome? Potentially, but I think it's a hard topic to deal with in a novel and it did bring out some interesting character nuances. Even the sometimes lackadaisical pacing could have been counterbalanced by the strong points of the story—typical King stuff like fun villains, gruesome body horror, and interesting side characters.

With some reflection, though, I think there were two main issues that led to this book leaving such a sour taste in my mouth. The first was that the whole book felt weirdly self-congratulatory. I found the side plots about the two Robinson children's writing endeavors, for example, to be mostly gratuitous and a little too starry-eyed. It was jarring to read about some of the horrors in store for the side characters while the two largely irrelevant side plots were about the Robinsons stacking up wins as young writers. Even making them both turn into writers seems self-indulgent! To me, it feels like King really loves these characters and expects us to love them the same way, but even though I've read most of the books in the Gibney-verse and enjoy the general lineup, I would much rather those characters had believable, interesting storylines than the ones we get in this book. The second thing that bothered me about this book was that it had an almost complete lack of suspense. I can understand the impulse to make a bold choice like revealing the villains and some of their motives early on in the story, but I think if you do that, you have to add some suspense later, and I didn't think that came through at all. The plot armor of all the main characters felt strong enough that even when Holly was staring death in the face, I didn't have any fear that she would come out of it much the worse for wear. I suppose the second point, then, is really more of a function of the first—it's hard to maintain a sense of energy and suspense when you're going off on constant digressions about characters who aren't really involved in the story!

Anyway, I worry a little that I'm not being fair to Mr. King. This is a fine book with some good pieces, it just doesn't hold a candle (in my little opinion) to some of his other recent work like The Outsider or The Institute.

Title: Hidden Pictures
Author: Jason Rekulak
My Review: This was a really fun little thriller/horror jaunt. I read it all on a plane and it was a perfect travel read. I'm a big fan of an unreliable narrator and I loved the tension that built up throughout this story as you wonder if Mallory is spiraling into some kind of addictive relapse or if she's really experiencing the supernatural. I thought the characters were well-drawn and the writing was solid, if unexceptional.

Title: The Covenant of Water
Author: Abraham   Verghese
My Review:
I really enjoyed this book—not quite ready to say I loved it but it was close (4.5 stars).

The highs:
- the author/narrator's love for Kerala came through strongly in the beautiful descriptions of the waterways and forests of Parambil. People say this a lot, but the setting really is a character in this one.
- the characters are rich, deep, and human with flaws and idiosyncrasies that make them memorable and captivating.
- the central storyline grows more and more powerful as the story extends over 70 years and you get a chance to know the more minor characters.

The slightly less high(s):
- the pacing can be uneven. Since the book spans such a dramatic range of time and place it can sometimes feel like a succession of "good thing happened, bad thing happened, good thing happened..." over and over without a clear sense of direction. This didn't really throw me off because these episodes never lasted long enough for me to get bored.
- the descriptions of surgeries and medical stuff writ large can be frustratingly detailed. You can tell the author loves medicine, but sometimes I wish he would just release a version for med students and a version for regular people.

Title: The Island
Author: Adrian McKinty
My Review: Good solid thriller with a few fun twists. I love the "unexpected character turns out to be a badass" trope and this one hit hard. I can't give it a super high number of stars because I wouldn't call it super high quality and it definitely started to lose my attention at points, but overall I was entertained.

Title: Demon Copperhead
Author: Barbara Kingsolver
My Review:
4.5 stars

This was a great read. As you'd expect from Kingsolver, it feels really faithful to the American South in a way that not many popular novels do—I'm used to shaking my head at a lazy trope or stilted piece of twangy dialogue every few pages when I read a novel with a piece set in North Carolina or Virginia. I loved the central story of Demon/Damon and thought it was beautifully told. Especially noteworthy was how the narration evolved to match his growing maturity. It was a really interesting device that I thought helped build a sense of connection with and empathy for Demon.

The theme I thought most about while reading this book was the notion of destiny and fate. Demon spends the whole story talking and thinking about his connection to his father and how his father died, and so it seems inevitable that he'll end up at the Devil's Bathtub at some point in the story. In parallel, we see the threads of fate tying up the residents of Lee county—the central question is how much agency the characters of the story have to escape them, and every character seems to have a different answer.

I'm excited to read this one again, and it makes me want to give David Copperfield a look as well.

Title: Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow
Author: Gabrielle Zevin
My Review: Good, entertaining book with a lot to recommend it.

Title: Lincoln in the Bardo
Author: George Saunders
My Review: The first 100 pages of this book really put me through the blender, but after having to struggle to keep myself reading for a while, I slowly found myself more and more absorbed and interested. At first, I shook my head at the ridiculousness of the constantly shifting narrators, tones, and themes, but soon I caught myself turning pages hoping for glimpses of my favorite characters and their lives. I thought the Bardo of Saunders's conception was a beautiful way of getting at the big questions about how we look back on our lives and those of others in retrospect. The Lincoln sections were heavy with grief, but also with energy and life. Lots to say about this one.

Title: The Fall Guy
Author: James Lasdun
My Review: Picked this up to read on a plane and honestly hated it. I thought the plot was fundamentally not that interesting and the psycho-sexual tension kind of thing was clumsy. I think I was also frustrated by how little self-knowledge the main character seemed to have. I understand that that's a feature of real life, but I find it inherently boring when a narrative is driven by a boring character that doesn't seem to have any real motives or goals.

Title: The Rabbit Hutch
Author: Tess Gunty
My Review:
3.5 stars.

This book felt like a fever-dream throughout—so full to the brim with textures, idiosyncratic characters, and imagined histories that it stands out in my memory in technicolor. I enjoyed the many perspectives style of narration, though I will say that it made the book feel almost more like a collection of vignettes than a cohesive narrative.

Title: No Plan B (Jack Reacher, #27)
Author: Lee Child
My Review: I picked this one up because I was tired of literary stuff and needed a break. It fits the form to a tee—always a great conspiracy going on and always entertaining.

Title: Lemon
Author: Kwon Yeo-Sun
My Review: Meh—felt like playing with a Russian nesting doll that went on forever.

Title: Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World
Author: Haruki Murakami
My Review:
I think I'm a little tired of Murakami. I liked this one in some ways, as I always do with his stuff. There's always something interesting going on and always some double-meaning to hunt for. But I'm tired of emotionless protagonists and I'm bored with stories I can't related to.

^ This is probably unnecessarily harsh. I love a meditation on consciousness. I just wish it were packaged a little differently.

Title: Birnam Wood
Author: Eleanor Catton
My Review: If I could give this a 3.5 stars I would. I enjoyed every minute of reading this book, but I don't think it's one that I'll come back to. I found the mystery elements of it a little lacking in plotting and pacing and the more literary elements weak in dramatic force. With that said, though, the writing is great, the characters are extremely interesting, and the twists and turns are fun to follow.

Title: Leviathan Wakes
Author: James S.A. Corey
My Review: Really fun! I loved that this was essentially a detective noir in space, much like the original Star Wars films are kind of westerns in space. Great world-building, solid characters, solid writing, not much to dislike.

Title: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd (Hercule Poirot, #4)
Author: Agatha Christie
My Review: Solid! I won't say any more to avoid spoilers :p

Title: The Bean Trees (Greer Family, #1)
Author: Barbara Kingsolver
My Review: I had a similar feeling about this book as I've had about previous Barbara Kingsolver books I've read. While reading it, I was drawn along nicely by the story. The writing was beautiful and evocative. The characters were well-rendered and had some real depth and heft to them. The plot took on some wonderfully complex issues. And yet, somehow, I don't find myself looking back on the book with anything like that "wow" feeling that I get when I've just finished something truly great. I think the issue with the story was that all of its dark depths are "off-screen," as it were. We hear about the terrors that Esperanza and Esteban go through in Guatemala; we reconstruct, later, the abuses Turtle suffered as a baby; we imagine the life that Mattie must lead: but the protagonist kind of floats along through them without really being tested. Taylor's greatest struggle, whether she can really be Turtle's mother, doesn't seem rendered with the same urgency and weight as the other off-screen stories, so the whole book feels a little lighter to me than it should.

Title: The Year of Magical Thinking
Author: Joan Didion
My Review: This is a book that—not to be too morbid about it—I think I need to revisit when I suffer a great loss. It's beautifully written, engaging, and has a wonderfully distinctive voice, but I think a lot of the emotional heft was muted for me (lucky me, knocking on wood as I write this). Instead, my main impression was that it felt like reading someone's diary—I was sometimes frustrated by the regular name-dropping of people I don't know and the feeling of being wrapped up in someone else's social circle without sufficient explanation of who these people are. That said, it struck me as a tremendously well-researched and thoughtful examination of grief. I'm not excited to revisit it (because of the circumstances that would require), but suffice it to say that I won't be sad about having to read it again (that feeling will be entirely separate).

Title: City of Thieves
Author: David Benioff
My Review: So much fun! Or maybe I should say very sad. Anyway, I really enjoyed this one. It was exactly what I was looking for after reading a couple of denser philosophy tomes recently. I found the growing friendship and love between Lev and Kolya to be touching and interesting, and I loved all of the discussion of Russian literature and music. I even enjoyed the love story between Lev and Vika, despite it feeling a little shoehorned in. I blame it on my personal weakness for the "hapless fool falls for dangerous woman with a kind heart" trope (am I manifesting?). I think the book strikes that difficult balance between centering on really tough, difficult, depressing subject matter and still maintaining a sense of levity and hope. Highly recommend it!

Title: Born a Crime: Stories from a South African Childhood
Author: Trevor Noah
My Review: I liked this book a lot! I found it a fascinating and compelling blend of humor, touching family drama, and powerful history. I read the book instead of listening to the audiobook—which I hear was a mistake—but I could still hear Trevor Noah's voice in my head telling some of the jokes.

Title: At the Existentialist Café
Author: Sarah Bakewell
My Review: Before reading this book, I would have said I was a sucker for existentialism—I'd still say so now, but with a new understanding of what that means. I found it really refreshing, interesting, and fun to read about the lives of the existentialists entwined with their philosophy and to learn about how they tried to live and embody their ideas. What compelling characters! I'm certainly going to be reading some Beauvoir, Sartre, and Kierkegaard (though I may skip the Heidegger) in the coming weeks and months.

Title: The Maidens
Author: Alex Michaelides
My Review: Eh. Convoluted thriller without a real sense of where it wanted to go—never had that awesome "aha" moment, much as it tried!

Author: Tom Fort

Title: Project Hail Mary
Author: Andy Weir
My Review: I thought this was a fine science fiction book—a little bit young adult-y, which isn't entirely a criticism.  It definitely held my attention, and I thought the premise was awesome. The memory loss and flashbacks added a little variety to that formula, but I didn't find that quite enough not to get a little bored with the constant here's an obstacle, now let's solve it with science! Maybe I'm a little too cynical, but that became a bit boring over time. I did love a lot of the details about alien creatures and civilizations—great world-building! All in all, I had fun with this one but I doubt it's a book I'll come back to or think much about in the future.

Title: The Secret History
Author: Donna Tartt
My Review: I read this book for the first time several years ago, maybe in 2016 or 2017, and it was great fun to re-read! I love the pace of this one, the growing sense of dread and unease Richard feels as he falls deeper and deeper into the morass surrounding Bunny's death, and the peculiar sense of displacement the novel evokes that is so distinctive to college life. I'm a big fan of the fractured timeline of the story and how the central conflict, the death of Bunny, is in the open from the beginning, while the surrounding events and context fill in slowly. Fundamentally, I think the story is about what it's like to feel alienated from oneself and one's surroundings, and the thrill and terror of finding people with whom to dissolve a little of that alienation. It doesn't beat The Goldfinch for me, but it's up there!

Title: The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo
Author: Taylor Jenkins Reid
My Review:
I liked this one! I thought the plot was great—really pulled me along, I loved the characters, and I enjoyed the romantic arcs throughout. I thought this also had the distinction of being one of the better "frame novels" I've read (forgive me, English teachers of my past and future, if I'm using that term wrongly). I really enjoyed the fact that the frame story and the framed story converged, and it was fun to try to predict how and when that would happen after the very early hints that it would.

My one qualm with this one was that I thought the writing was just ok. It read a bit like a teen beach read, with some overwrought dialogue and overly florid descriptions of the various love affairs. The faux news articles, especially, read a little like book reports. It also had some of my worst pet peeve in writing, which is TFC (Too Few Contractions)—when dialogue between characters includes unnatural lack of contractions.

Other than that, though, not much to complain about—read it all in one long sitting on a flight :)

Title: The Little Friend
Author: Donna Tartt
My Review:
This is definitely my least favorite Donna Tartt novel. First off, some things I loved:

- the atmospherics of small-town Mississippi in the early 70s—snakes, heat, Bible study, meth, the works.
- Harriet's perspective (so relatable to me as a former bookish, analytical, awkward kid with a weakness for assuming I knew better than everyone else)
- the deep, sympathetic characters. I especially loved Edie, the matriarch with a will of iron who is unwilling to see or incapable of seeing the many ways in which her lack of empathy hurts those around her, and the whole Ratliff family, whose cruelties to one another I often found heartbreaking.
- the portrayal of how grief can seep into every person in a family in different, and often contradictory, ways.

The main thing I didn't like about it was that I found it overwrought and a little aimless. The descriptions of, well, everything, tend to wander. From the way that crape myrtle grows on a trellis to Harriet's processing of the departure of her beloved nanny Ida to the many, many reminiscences of the family's old mansion, the narration observes everything in painstaking detail, without ever quite deciding *why* it's doing so. The decision to center the plot around Harriet and Hely means that the reader is tied to the logical leaps and jumps of children, which, for me, takes away some of the sense of momentum of the story. After the first few pages, which so poignantly and terrifyingly set up the central emotional hook of Robin's death, the story bogs down in a seemingly endless maelstrom of familial grief and neglect. The character studies, beautiful as they are, weren't enough for me to feel engaged in the story, and by the end, I felt like I was slogging through.

Title: In Five Years
Author: Rebecca Serle
My Review:
In Five Years was a solid read. In this kind of story, where you know some of the ending at the beginning, the joy, for me, is always in trying to figure out where you think things are headed and how they're going to get there. The true test of such a book is how enjoyable it is to keep reading even if you do happen to figure it out, and this one passed that test for me. The story's central relationship was so strong and well established that it pulled me through in a very quick read.

While I was perfectly happy to finish it, the book felt a bit formulaic to me. Dannie, with her over-the-top, perfectly designed life, seemed a little ridiculous at times. That helped to add weight to the lifestyle shift she goes through at the end of the story, but I got a bit tired at yet another description of why Dannie loves her powerful corporate job. Maybe I just don't know a lot of those corporate types (:P). Bella, too, was more of an archetype than a fully-realized person, and other than Dannie and Bella, the characters in the novel are almost entirely flat. That's ok (it's not a long book, so there's only so much real estate for character-building), but I think I would have been more captivated if there were other characters I could root for more strongly.

I doubt I'll read this again, but I did enjoy it, especially for a quick and casual read!

Title: Everything I Never Told You
Author: Celeste Ng
My Review:
I loved this book! After reading Little Fires Everywhere earlier this year, I was eager to read another from Celeste Ng. Even so, I was a little surprised by how much I enjoyed this one, given that Little Fires Everywhere got more hype (from what I saw).

I love a good story about a dysfunctional family, but they can be a bit of a risky proposition. In a not-so-good family drama, all of the problems in the story can be resolved from the outset with a good long conversation and maybe some therapy—and crucially, there's no hint to the reader as to why that conversation doesn't happen. In Everything I Never Told You, though, it's painfully clear what it is that's getting in the way of the happy resolution that everyone wants. All of the characters in this story are lying to one another, but admitting that to themselves would mean abandoning the images they've built up about both themselves and their loved ones. It's a crippling state to be in, and it's one that I think anyone reading the book can empathize with.

The character who suffers most from this self-suppression is Lydia, who, ironically, is also the character best able to perceive the desires of her family members, but I was equally heartbroken at the plight of those around her. Her younger sister, Hannah, just wants to be loved and cared for, but has become a reclusive little "mouse" in order to give her parents what they want, which is unfettered access to their favorite child, Lydia. Jack, the neighbor whom Lydia befriends, is secretly in love with her older brother Nathaniel, but can't show it. Nathaniel buries himself in his schoolwork and a fascination with astronauts so that he doesn't have to confront his father, who is cruel to Nathaniel mostly because Nathaniel is too like him. No one is safe from the weight of their own, and others', expectations, and I think that that's what this book is about at its core—the expectations that we have of ourselves and our family members, that communities have about one another (the Lee family being the only Asian-American family in their whitebread suburban town), that we have of the future.

This review is at serious risk of turning into a five-paragraph essay, so I'm going to close it out here and just say that reading this book makes me really grateful to have a family that doesn't deal so heavily in expectation.

Title: The Last Thing He Told Me (Hannah Hall, #1)
Author: Laura Dave
My Review:
I thought this book was a fine mystery/thriller with a relatively interesting set of twists and reveals, but I didn't enjoy the style or the pacing. One of my pet peeves in mystery novels in general is when we, the readers, are too far inside the protagonist's head—that is, when the protagonist has an impossibly rich and detailed internal monologue that essentially carries the reader along without letting them do any of the work for themself. For me, it dampens the fun of the mystery when I don't have to do any real thinking to figure out what's going on! This book definitely went too far in that direction for me—at times, it felt more like reading an instruction manual than a novel. Another thing I wasn't a huge fan of was that the core mystery of the story is revealed within a relatively small section of the book in the middle. The sections before and after that are mostly rote following along.

With that said, there were pieces of the book that I really enjoyed, too! The developing relationship between Hannah and Bailey was genuine and fun, and I liked the "antagonist" characters revealed near the end—I just wish they could have had a little bit more time to develop. Of course, the initial hook of the disappearing husband, the inscrutable note, and the bag of cash was immediately absorbing, and over all, I thought the writing was clean and fun to read. Not a book that I'm likely to read again, but I had a good time with it!

Title: Klara and the Sun
Author: Kazuo Ishiguro
My Review:
I really enjoyed this book. Something about the way Klara saw the world really struck a chord with me—I thought it was a convincing guess at what consciousness might feel like as an android, though of course the joy of this story is that it's speculative. I loved how Ishiguro didn't feel pressured to fully explain all of the nuances of exactly how Klara's perception works, e.g. the "boxes" that she talks about as a way to describe her vision. In fact, I thought one of my favorite pieces of this story was how thoroughly Ishiguro drops the reader into the story. It was a little more work to try to piece together a coherent vision of how the society in the story works, but I think that that allows the reader more leeway to project their own hopes and fears for the future onto that society and its mechanics.

In the end, though, what really absorbed me was the emotional heft of the relationships at the story's core—Klara and Josie, Josie and Rick, Josie and her mother, Josie's mother and Rick's. Seeing those relationships from the point of view of Klara, who is ignorant of some of the history and context of the characters but is also unencumbered by things like ego or pride, was, I found, a touching light in which to view them. Even absent all of the interesting questions the book raises about technology, humanity, and progress, this would have been a beautiful book about parents trying their best to make a good life for their children, friends trying to make their own way in the world while staying true to their companions, and consciousness (alone!) trying to make sense of its place in the world.

Title: Journey Under the Midnight Sun
Author: Keigo Higashino
My Review:
My enthusiasm for this book started off low and slowly grew until by the end, I was pretty hooked. The tactic of focusing on different characters in different points of their lives in successive chapters made it a little difficult for me to feel connected to the characters at the beginning, but I would say that that was worth it for the delicious sense of each chapter adding a new facet to the story. The plot was intricate, well-crafted, and full of interesting characters, and I enjoyed the setting in the early days of the internet era, where the notion of what a computer could do was changing by the year. The overall feeling, for me, was one of entanglement in a giant spiderweb, where the truth of the story was the hapless insect slowly being wrapped, chapter by chapter, into a bite-sized bundle. The only thing I would have changed is that I didn't feel like I got to know the antagonists at all. That seemed to me to be by design, but the emotional impact of the final reveal was less intense than I felt it should have been because I didn't really know the characters involved.

Semi-unrelated note: This is the second thriller/mystery novel I've read that was originally written in Japanese (after Bullet Train by Kotaro Isaka). I'm not sure whether it's a feature of Japanese novels writ large or the translations I've read or just these two novels, but I found both to be extremely matter of fact and light on stylistic flair. The plot, far more so than the writing, was the centerpiece. It really makes me wonder if that's the way the two come off in the original Japanese.
